title: Moong Dal Dhokla: The Protein-Packed Gujarati Snack You Can Make Without Besan
excerpt: This steamed, no-fermentation version of dhokla swaps traditional chickpea flour for soaked moong dal, delivering 14 grams of protein per serving in under 30 minutes.

  • No overnight fermentation needed; soak dal for 30 minutes to 4 hours.
  • Steaming takes only 10-12 minutes, ideal for quick meals.
  • All ingredients are easily available at Indian grocery stores worldwide.

  • Moong dal dhokla delivers about 14 grams of protein per serving — nearly as much as two eggs — while remaining low in fat and easy to digest.
  • The recipe requires no overnight fermentation; soaking the dal for 30 minutes to 4 hours is enough to get started.
  • Steaming takes just 10-12 minutes, making it a quick breakfast or tiffin option for busy weekday mornings.
  • All ingredients — yellow moong dal, curd, green chillies, fruit salt (Eno) — are available at any Indian grocery store abroad.

Why Moong Dal Instead of Besan?

The classic Gujarati dhokla — the spongy, tangy, steamed square that anchors breakfasts and tea-time plates across western India — is traditionally made with besan (chickpea flour). But a growing number of home cooks and nutritionists are turning to moong dal as the base, and for good reason.

Split yellow moong dal is one of the lightest pulses in Indian cooking. It is easier to digest than chickpea flour, lower in carbohydrates and richer in bioavailable protein. A single serving of moong dal dhokla delivers roughly 14 grams of protein and about 220 calories, with just 3.3 grams of fat. For vegetarians tracking their protein intake — a common concern for Indians abroad navigating Western diets — it is one of the most efficient snacks available.

The texture differs too. Where besan dhokla is dense and holds its shape firmly, moong dal dhokla comes out softer and more delicate, with a subtle earthiness that pairs well with a sharp green chutney or a sweet tamarind drizzle.

The Recipe

Ingredients (serves 4):

1 cup yellow moong dal (split, without skin) · ½ cup fresh curd (dahi) · 2-3 green chillies · 1 tsp ginger paste · 2 tsp besan (for binding) · ¼ tsp turmeric · a pinch of asafoetida (hing) · 1 tsp sugar · salt to taste · 1 tsp fruit salt (Eno) or ½ tsp baking soda · 2 tsp oil

For tempering: 1 tbsp oil · 1 tsp mustard seeds · 1 tsp sesame seeds · a pinch of hing · 2 green chillies (slit) · 8-10 curry leaves

Garnish: chopped coriander · grated fresh coconut

Step by Step

Soak: Wash the moong dal thoroughly and soak in water for 30 minutes to 4 hours. Longer soaking yields a smoother batter.

Grind: Drain the dal and blend with green chillies, ginger and minimal water into a smooth, thick batter — not runny. The consistency should resemble idli batter.

Mix: Transfer to a bowl. Fold in the curd, besan, turmeric, hing, sugar and salt. The batter should be pourable but not watery.

Steam: Just before steaming, add the fruit salt (Eno) and 2 teaspoons of water. Mix gently — do not overmix, as this deflates the air bubbles that give dhokla its sponge. Pour immediately into a greased thali or steaming plate. Steam on high heat for 10-12 minutes, until a toothpick comes out clean.

Temper: Heat oil in a small pan. Add mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add sesame seeds, hing, slit green chillies and curry leaves. Sauté for 30 seconds and pour evenly over the steamed dhokla.

Serve: Let the dhokla cool slightly, cut into squares or diamonds, and garnish with coriander and coconut. Serve warm with green chutney.

Tips From the Experts

According to Tarla Dalal's test kitchen, the most common mistake is adding too much water during grinding — excess moisture makes the dhokla dense and prevents proper cooking. The fruit salt must be added at the very last moment; mixing it in early allows the carbon dioxide to escape before the batter hits the steamer.

Greasing the thali with ghee rather than oil makes demoulding easier and adds a faint richness. For a more nutritious version, add a handful of chopped fenugreek leaves (methi) to the batter — it increases the fibre and iron content while giving the dhokla a subtle bitter note that balances the sweetness of the tempering.

The Cultural Context

Dhokla belongs to the broader family of Gujarati farsan — steamed and fried snacks that form the backbone of the state's famously vegetarian cuisine. In Gujarat, dhokla is as likely to appear at a breakfast table as it is at a wedding reception or a railway platform stall. The moong dal variation, while less common in commercial settings, has roots in home kitchens where grandmothers soaked and ground dal long before packaged besan was widely available.

Quick and Easy Preparation
›Soak moong dal for 30 minutes to 4 hours.
›Steam for 10-12 minutes.
›No fermentation required.
›Ideal for busy mornings.
